messages.author: 6b3b475e6af83898
messages.subject: Reflection invariance
parts:
For an ideal point model (for simplicity, call it IRT) I’m working on, I’d like to let discrimination be positive or negative, since unpooled analyses I’ve run show that some discriminations do seem to take on different signs in different countries, and I don’t want to assume that my reverse coding will always be right.

In ARM, it’s recommended to add a predictor x coding one person (or item) as positive, the other negative, the rest 0, and estimate an orienting parameter d such that discrimination[i] = x[i]*d+eta[i].

I gave this approach a shot in Stan (checking it against the implementation in the ARM example posted at github), and the models are failing to converge after long, long runs, and often not even generating estimated discriminations of opposite signs for the items chosen! (I chose those items both because of prior knowledge about the nature of the items and because a standard IRT analysis using ltm shows them to be the items with the most positive and negative discriminations, respectively).

I’ve also experimented with constraining the priors, using a loop in the model section specifying:

for (i in 1:K){
if (x[i] == 1) gamma[i] ~ normal(0,1)T[0,];
else if (x[i] == -1) gamma[i] ~ normal(0,1)T[,0];
else gamma[i] ~ normal(0,1);
}

It converges more quickly, but gives me results that don’t make sense (i.e., other questions that I know should have large, negative discriminations are estimated with large, positive discriminations).

When I reverse-code the items and give gamma a log-normal prior, the results match my expectations based on the ltm analysis, which makes me confident that the rest of the model is fine.

Can anyone offer suggestions of other ways to address reflection invariance in Stan? Or a different way that I might think about this problem that would obviate the issue?

Thanks,
Josh

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Reflection invariance
parts:
It helps if you send more of the Stan code.

I'm guessing the problem you're having is with constraints.
Parameters need to be declared with constraints that match
their support. Stan's limited constraint language makes it
hard to do what Andrew was suggesting in ARM (if I understand
corectly), namely constraining one element of an array to
be positive and one negative.

The natural solution in Stan is this:

parameters {
real<lower=0> gamma_pos;
real<upper=0> gamma_neg;
vector[K-2] gamma_rest;
}
transformed parameters {
vector[K] gamma;
gamma[1] <- gamma_pos;
gamma[2] <- gamma_neg;
for (k in 3:K)
gamma[k] <- gamma_rest[k-2];
}
model {
gamma_pos ~ normal(0,1);
gamma_neg ~ normal(0,1);
gamma_rest ~ normal(0,1);

You don't need the truncations as they're built into
the constraints (though you would need them and the model
would need to be made more complex. All the above would
be more efficient as just:

gamma ~ normal(0,1);

Sorry it's so clunky --- it's only to deal with the varying constraints.

- Bob

for (k in 3:K)

messages.author: 6b3b475e6af83898
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Reflection invariance
parts:
Thanks for this. I got it implemented and played with it, and have a system that’s working well.

In the end, I took a different direction, which I’ll report here for the benefit of anyone else struggling with a comparable situation.

The problem I kept having, even using solutions like the one below, is that the gammas kept getting pushed toward zero (and if I allowed sigma_gamma to vary, /it/ got pushed toward zero). In the end, I realized that it was because I had a bimodal distribution, with one mode on the negative side for the reverse-coded items, and another on the positive side for the others. That caused all the problems one would expect. So I changed tack, reverse-coding the items I knew ought to be reverse-coded, and estimated

gamma ~ normal(mu_gamma,sigma_gamma);

I obliged the hyperprior mu_gamma to be > sigma_gamma/2, to keep it away from zero and ensure that most of the density of the parameters would be positive, and gave it a prior of cauchy(1,5). There’s no restriction on gamma itself, but those constraints on the priors and hyperpriors ensured that there was very little density on the negative side of any of the gammas estimated.

If I didn’t have prior knowledge that would let me reverse-code items, I’d probably have to do some sort of mixture model, I guess, or use a extremely diffuse (or uniform) prior on gamma and orient it as Bob suggested.

Thanks,
Josh

"## priors
for (i in 1:40){ x[i] ~ dnorm(0,1) }

for (i in 67:100){ x[i] ~ dnorm(0,1) }

for (n in 1:N){

}
}

parts:
On Tuesday, July 22, 2014 1:46:10 PM UTC-4, Y Kenan wrote:
I am pretty new to STAN and trying to replicate Jackman's "legislators" openbugs code for ideal point estimation in stan. Jackman specifies two constant ideal points; one for the left and one for the right. I couldn't achieve this in stan. 

The priors in openbugs are specified as follows:
"## priors
for (i in 1:40){ x[i] ~ dnorm(0,1) }
for (i in 42:65){ x[i] ~ dnorm(0,1) }
for (i in 67:100){ x[i] ~ dnorm(0,1) }
x[41] <- -1.0  ## Kennedy on the left
x[66] <- 1.0   ## Helms on the right  "

This means that the ideal points for Kennedy and Helms are fixed rather than being random variables. So, the same thing needs to be done in Stan for Pelosi and Bachman.
 
votes_code<- '

data {
  int<lower=1> J;              // number of legislators
  int<lower=1> K;              // number of votes
  int<lower=1> N;              // number of observations
  int<lower=1,upper=J> jj[N];  // legislator for observation n
  int<lower=1,upper=K> kk[N];  // vote for observation n
  int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];   // position for observation n
}
parameters {    
  real alpha[K];
real beta[K];

real<upper=-1> xx_pelosi;
  real<lower=1> xx_bachman;
Eliminate these two but keep xx_rest

real xx_rest[J-2]; 
  
}
transformed parameters { 
  real xx[J]; 
  xx[268] <- xx_pelosi; 
  xx[394] <- xx_bachman;
Change those to -1.0 and 1.0 respectively. The loop would be less convoluted if the data were sorted with Pelosi first and Bachman last or something like that.

for (j in 1:(J-178)) 
    xx[j] <- xx_rest[J-178]; 
for (j in (J-176):(J-52)) 
    xx[j] <- xx_rest[J-220]; 
for (j in (J-50):J) 
    xx[j] <- xx_rest[J-394]; 

}   
model {
for (k in 1:K){ alpha[k] ~ normal(0,0.4);         // informative true prior
}
for (k in 1:K){beta[k] ~ normal(0,0.4);          // informative true prior
}
 
{xx_pelosi ~ normal(-1,1);          // informative true prior
}
{xx_bachman ~ normal(1,1);          // informative true prior
}

You don't need braces here but moreover you don't need xx_pelosi and xx_bachman to be random variables. These priors do orient the latent variable from liberal to conservative but to be equivalent to Simon's approach they should be fixed.

Ben

messages.author: 6b3b475e6af83898
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Reflection invariance
parts:
To simplify the loop somewhat (or at least generalize it), xx_rest could be of size J-2, so you could just do xx_rest ~ normal(0,1);

Then you could have two items specified in the data block specifying an index for a known liberal and another for a known conservative, and when populating the transformed parameter, use the fix values when you get to those indices. You'd also have to mess with the index to xx_rest as it gets copied over to x, subtracting 1 from the loop index if you're over the liberal point, and subtracting also if you're over the conservative index.

Doing that lets you avoid writing assumptions about the structure of the data into the code, and more easily experiment with different ways of orienting the model, or different subsets of the data, without recompiling. I wonder if, by combining the 3 normal(0,1) calls into a single call, you
might not speed things up a tad.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Reflection invariance
parts:
You should have run into trouble parsing here:

> theta[j]<-theta_rest[26:59];

There's no R-like array slicing syntax in Stan.

What you want to do is actually use the loop structure
you set up, as in:

> parameters{
> ...
> real theta_rest[J-2]; //ideal point (ability of j)
> }

> transformed parameters{
> real theta[J];
> for (j in 1:24)
> theta[j]<-theta_rest[1:24];
> for (j in 26:59)
> theta[j]<-theta_rest[26:59];
> for (j in 61:102)
> theta[j]<-theta_rest[61:102];
> theta[25]<- -1; //constraint on Durbin
> theta[60]<- 1; //constraint on Demint
> }


You just need to keep track of the offset into theta:

> transformed parameters{
> real theta[J];
> for (j in 1:24)
> theta[j] <- theta_rest[j];
> theta[25]<- -1; //constraint on Durbin
> for (j in 26:59)
> theta[j] <- theta_rest[j-1];
> theta[60]<- 1; //constraint on Demint
> for (j in 61:102)
> theta[j]<-theta_rest[j-2];
> }

You don't need to do it in order, but I find it's easier
to scan that you've got the right ranges that way.

I don't like the 25 and 60 or the 102 being hard-coded
into the model.

Is the point of fixing two points to constrain the overall
scale? You already have a pretty gith constraint with

> theta_rest ~ normal(0,1);

but not incompatible with setting extremes to -1 and 1 (assuming
those two are extreme points).

You might want to put a bit tighter priors on alpha and beta.
25 is a huge coefficient for a logistic regression.

- Bob

parts: Yes, it's declared here:
> int<lower=1,upper=J> j[N]; //legislator for observation n

You can't reuse variables declared in any of the blocks because
they remain in scope for every block after they're declared.

We decided to disallow variable hiding by catching it in
the parser so there weren't any nasty surprises later.

- Bob
